items.followUp: Write four differences between an element and a compound.

rubric.why: Compounds form through chemical combination, whereas mixtures form through physical mixing.
rubric.description: Contrasts how compounds and mixtures are formed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that elements are chemically combined in a compound but substances are physically mixed in a mixture.

rubric.why: A compound has a fixed composition, while a mixture can have variable proportions.
rubric.description: Contrasts the composition of compounds and mixtures.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving the fixed-versus-variable composition contrast.

rubric.why: A compound has properties different from its constituents, while mixture components retain their properties.
rubric.description: Compares the properties of compounds and mixtures.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving this contrast.

rubric.why: Compounds are separated by chemical methods; mixture components can be separated by physical methods.
rubric.description: Compares how compounds and mixtures are separated.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly contrasting the separation methods.

rubric.why: Pure compounds have characteristic fixed melting and boiling points; mixtures generally do not.
rubric.description: Contrasts the melting or boiling points of compounds and mixtures.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct comparison of their melting or boiling points.

modelAnswer: A compound is formed when elements chemically combine; a mixture is formed by physically mixing substances.
A compound has a fixed composition, with its elements in a definite ratio; a mixture has a variable composition.
A compound has properties different from those of its constituent elements; the components of a mixture retain their properties.
A compound can be separated into its elements by chemical methods; the components of a mixture can be separated by physical methods.
A pure compound has a fixed melting and boiling point; mixtures generally melt over a range and do not have fixed boiling points.

items.followUp: Explain the formation of a coordinate covalent bond in the ammonium ion, using a dot-and-cross diagram or a Lewis representation.

rubric.why: In a coordinate covalent bond, one atom supplies both electrons in the shared pair.
rubric.description: Defines a coordinate covalent bond by the source of its shared electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that one atom donates both electrons of the shared pair.

rubric.why: Ammonia is the electron-pair donor and H⁺ is the acceptor in the ammonium-ion example.
rubric.description: Identifies the donor and acceptor in the ammonia example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying ammonia and H⁺ in this example.

rubric.why: Water is the electron-pair donor and H⁺ is the acceptor in the hydronium-ion example.
rubric.description: Identifies the donor and acceptor in the water example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying water and H⁺ in this example.

rubric.why: The examples show formation of NH₄⁺ and H₃O⁺ from ammonia or water and H⁺.
rubric.description: Gives the products formed in both examples.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for showing both formation equations or their equivalent representations.

modelAnswer: A coordinate covalent bond is formed when one atom donates both electrons of the shared pair to another atom.
In ammonia, nitrogen donates its lone pair to H⁺: NH₃ + H⁺ ⟶ NH₄⁺.
In water, oxygen donates a lone pair to H⁺: H₂O + H⁺ ⟶ H₃O⁺.
In each product, the donated pair forms a coordinate covalent bond.

items.followUp: What are isotopes? Describe the isotopes of oxygen and give their numbers of protons and neutrons.

rubric.why: Isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
rubric.description: Defines isotopes by their atomic and mass numbers.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating both that the atomic number is the same and the mass number differs.

rubric.why: The commonly described carbon isotopes have mass numbers 12, 13 and 14.
rubric.description: Identifies the mass numbers of the carbon isotopes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving all three carbon isotope mass numbers.

rubric.why: The three hydrogen isotopes are protium, deuterium and tritium, with mass numbers 1, 2 and 3.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming all three isotopes or giving their mass numbers.

rubric.why: The hydrogen isotopes contain zero, one and two neutrons, respectively.
rubric.description: Matches the hydrogen isotopes to their neutron numbers.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly matching all three hydrogen isotopes to their neutron numbers.

rubric.why: The two common chlorine isotopes have mass numbers 35 and 37.
rubric.description: Identifies the mass numbers of the common chlorine isotopes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving both chlorine isotope mass numbers.

modelAnswer: Isotopes are atoms of the same element having the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
Carbon has three isotopes: carbon-12 has 6 neutrons, carbon-13 has 7 neutrons and carbon-14 has 8 neutrons; each has 6 protons.
Hydrogen has three isotopes: protium (¹H) has 1 proton and 0 neutrons, deuterium (²H) has 1 proton and 1 neutron, and tritium (³H) has 1 proton and 2 neutrons.
Chlorine has two common isotopes: chlorine-35 has 17 protons and 18 neutrons, while chlorine-37 has 17 protons and 20 neutrons.
